title: Why is there such a vicious hair trigger reaction to anything AI made?
author: No_Departure7494
selftext:
It comes off as extremely pretentious. Say some guy wanted to make a racing game for him and his buddies, perhaps using cars that aren't commonly found in a videogame to begin with, somehow this is considered rage inducing to the purists. 

But why? It's a videogame. Do you really think the person at behind that creation was going to spend years learning to code or mastering game design? This shit is extremely demanding. 

It seems like a mindless reflex at this rate. That they've got no ability to differentiate total trash that someone wants to sell on steam and cash in on genuine slop vs. a creation that was once out of reach for the average person who could NEVER dedicate their time to learning this. As a hobby or a profession.

comments.author: RUSuper
comments.body: Cuz it's free karma and gives a person feeling of moral superiority to say "AI bad"...

comments.author: Limp_Bus3865
comments.body: virtue signaling and usually people who are talking like this are in denial and were doing something that ai started to replace. The water argument is just their retionalization. The same people who are fine having nice things which are made by slaves in third world countries and fine with water usage for cooling servers without ai, but suddenly ai is the biggest problem lol

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body:
Because they're internalized their hatred and have manufactured a personality around hating AI and not loving something. It gives them a false sense that they are cultured or have taste - they don't need to have discernment as the very act of pointing out that something "looks AI" is enough to give them the dopamine hit of thinking they made some interesting observation or have formed a useful critique.

Now couple that with the sense of superiority that hating AI is tied with "saving the planet" because of such and such overblown environmental concerns and you have a fundamentalist who will never be able to change their opinion because that would mean admitting they were wrong and foolish.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
There are two kinds of hair triggers out there. 

One is the people who have moral objections and think they have a duty to avoid AI and call it out. 

The other is from all the low-quality AI-generated media out there. All those text posts, fruit videos, etc. We know it sucks. When we see the suckiness, there’s a hair trigger response because we’re just so tired and overwhelmed.

replies.author: TrueFireOSP
replies.body:
For some it's moral about the moral issues around AI data centers causing locals to get priced out of homes due to rising energy and water costs associated to the data centers. People using AI for this just validates the Corpo's that AI is being used for proper use cases. When it's just people creating wasteful prototypes that will never see the light of the day or be remembered a month from now.

I personally am stuck 50/50 on it. At work AI has really helped me deliver on things that my IT org couldn't deliver properly for years. I am more self reliant for IT things now.

But at home.. I have a moral issue with me having a fart and thinking "oh I should give anthropic $ for my fart idea".

I appreciate good AIgames though. Some people have had some really cool stuff. But unfortunately that's a minority. Most posts are crappy concepts that a basic developer could come up with without having a negative long term impact on society/environment.

comments.author: wslk
comments.body:
The problem tends not to be with the work itself - but instead the mindset of people who have made what tends to be a feature MVP with AI - “hey do you think this is good!?” 

These posts tread the line between, engagement bait and sincerity and it is hard to tell where the author actually is. In my mind it isn’t so different than a grown adult sharing a crayola color inside the lines sketch from a fast food joint and asking for people for feedback online. If the person wanted feedback they should be making a sincere effort before asking for engagement. 

After all many of these posts probably have LESS effort put into them than a color between the lines sketch.

comments.author: UnmarkedWestDev
comments.body:
I’m absolutely not anti-AI, I use it every day and it's even professionally my area of expertise. But they’re not completely wrong.

Not because of AI. Because of the lazy, mindless, irritating and sometimes blatantly unethical way so many people use it. We see it all the time, even in this sub: walls of copy-pasted Claude text, asset flips with a fake trailer, a weekend of prompting sold on Steam as a “passion project”. That’s what people picture when they hear “AI game”, and that’s what they’re reacting to.

Nobody should care about your racing game for you and your buddies. The problem is the flood. AI doesn’t entitle incompetent people to fill the world with their noise.

And AI has nothing to do with it. There are humans behind all this.

comments.author: Deyachtifier
comments.body:
As a broad generality people dislike things that are made cheaply but sold in competition with standard or premium goods.  The AI disdain reads very similarly to the "foreign manufacturer" disdain I've seen through my life - from cars, to appliances, to woodworking tools, house building, etc.  When I was a kid, "Japanese cars" were treated with the same contempt that "Chinese EV cars" are today, even though the Japanese cars then were already better than American ones, and today's Chinese EVs seem to be pretty darn competitive themselves.

Many of the arguments against AI are the same, too - taking jobs away from American / human workers, skirting regulations that make domestic / human companies less competitive, "just makes the rich owner class richer at our expense", etc.

That said, many of the worries did in fact come to pass, but they were kind of inevitable given how the world economy works.  I personally feel the same is true with AI development - people can complain and say it's not what they want, but that isn't going to change the fact that it's going to happen regardless.

The trick, though, is the same thing the Japanese and Chinese manufacturers realized - the path forward needs to be a relentless growth of \*quality\*, not just stick with "cheap".  Same challenge exists for AI games: focus on not on minimizing effort/expense but on maximizing quality, and the anti-AI arguments will get overridden by consumers that just want the best options.
